title: Things to Do in the Sundarbans: Creek Safaris, Watchtowers & Village Life
seoTitle: Things to Do in the Sundarbans: Boat Safaris & More | Kudozz Club
description: Things to do in the Sundarbans: boat safaris through mangrove creeks, watchtowers at Sajnekhali, Sudhanyakhali, Dobanki and Netidhopani, the Dobanki canopy walk, crocodiles and birds, Bonbibi folk theatre, village walks in Gosaba and fresh Bengali fish.
dek: The world's largest mangrove forest, a maze of tidal rivers and islands at the mouth of the Ganga and Brahmaputra, home to swimming tigers and resilient island communities.
searchIntent: Travellers from Kolkata and beyond planning a two- or three-day Sundarbans boat trip and wondering what they will see and do.

hero.caption: The Sundarbans

intro: The Sundarbans spread across the delta of the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Meghna in India and Bangladesh. The Indian part, in South 24 Parganas district of West Bengal, includes Sundarbans National Park, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987, and a tiger reserve. Its tidal channels, mudflats and mangrove islands change with every tide.

The Royal Bengal tigers here are famous for swimming between islands and are rarely seen; most visitors never spot one. The real pleasure of things to do in the Sundarbans is slower: gliding through narrow creeks on a boat, climbing watchtowers, seeing estuarine crocodiles, spotted deer, monitor lizards and kingfishers, and learning about the lives of islanders who share the forest with tigers.

A two-night boat or lodge package from Kolkata is the practical minimum. October to March is the best season. Entry into the reserve requires a Forest Department permit, usually arranged by registered operators.

items.name: Take a creek safari

image.alt: Tourist boat among mangroves in Sundarbans National Park
image.caption: A creek safari

body: Most time in the Sundarbans is spent on a motor boat, following wide rivers and narrow side creeks through the mangroves. Guides watch the mudbanks for tiger pugmarks, crocodiles basking at low tide and deer at the forest edge. Visitors are not allowed to step onto the forest floor except at designated watchtower sites.
Tide timings shape the day; low tide exposes the mudflats and makes wildlife easier to spot.

items.name: Look for crocodiles, deer and birds
body: Estuarine crocodiles, spotted deer, rhesus macaques, water monitors, wild boar and mudskippers are commonly seen. The Sundarbans are also rich in birds, including several species of kingfisher, herons, egrets, brahminy kites and white-bellied sea eagles. Winter brings migrants.

items.name: Keep your tiger expectations realistic
body: Tigers here are elusive and live in dense mangrove. Sightings do happen, usually from boats or watchtowers, but they are rare. Enjoy the forest for itself; a tiger is a bonus.

items.name: Visit Sajnekhali
body: Sajnekhali, the main entry point, has the forest office where permits are checked, a watchtower, a mangrove interpretation centre, a crocodile and turtle enclosure, and a small temple to Bonbibi, the forest goddess.

items.name: Climb Sudhanyakhali and Dobanki watchtowers
body: Sudhanyakhali watchtower overlooks a freshwater pond where animals come to drink, and it is considered one of the better spots for sightings. Dobanki has a canopy walk, a caged elevated walkway of about half a kilometre through the mangroves, a few metres above the ground.

items.name: See Netidhopani
body: Netidhopani, deeper in the reserve, has a watchtower and the ruins of a centuries-old temple linked to the folk tale of Behula. Access depends on permits and the route of your boat.

items.name: Watch a Bonbibi performance
body: Islanders of all faiths worship Bonbibi, the goddess who protects people in the forest. Many lodges arrange evening performances of Bonbibi's story and local folk music by village troupes.

items.name: Walk through a village
body: Gosaba, Pakhirala, Bali and other islands have villages of fishermen, honey collectors and farmers. A guided walk shows embankments against the tide, ponds, paddy fields and daily life. In Gosaba, the bungalow of Sir Daniel Hamilton, who set up cooperative settlements here in the early 20th century, can be seen.

items.name: Eat fresh Bengali fish
body: Meals on the boat or at lodges usually feature fresh fish and prawns from local waters, cooked in Bengali style with mustard, rice and dal. Vegetarian meals are available on request.

items.name: Learn about the honey collectors
body: Every spring, licensed groups of mouals (honey collectors) enter the forest to gather wild honey, one of the most dangerous jobs in the delta because of tigers. Some villages sell Sundarbans honey, and local guides can explain how communities have adapted to living beside the forest, including the cooperatives and self-help groups working on alternative livelihoods.

byTraveller.text: A two-night package with a comfortable lodge, the Sajnekhali centre, the Dobanki canopy walk and a village walk.
Three nights on a boat covering several watchtowers, with early starts at low tide.
Winter mornings on the creeks for mist, birds and the light on the mangroves.

oneDay: Leave Kolkata early for Godkhali jetty and board the boat. Visit Sajnekhali for permits and the interpretation centre, then cruise the creeks to Sudhanyakhali watchtower in the afternoon. Return to your lodge for a Bonbibi performance in the evening.
tips: Most trips start at Godkhali jetty, about three to four hours by road from Kolkata.
Book with registered operators; they arrange permits, boats and guides.
Carry insect repellent, sunscreen, a hat and binoculars.
Avoid the monsoon (June to September), when the water is rough and cyclones are possible.
Mobile signal is weak or absent in much of the reserve; tell family your itinerary before you leave.

faqs.q: What are the best things to do in the Sundarbans?
faqs.a: Take boat safaris through the creeks, visit the watchtowers at Sajnekhali, Sudhanyakhali and Dobanki, walk the canopy walk, look for crocodiles and birds, and see village life and Bonbibi performances.

faqs.q: Can I see a tiger in the Sundarbans?
faqs.a: It is possible but rare. The forest is dense and the tigers are elusive.

faqs.q: How many days are needed for the Sundarbans?
faqs.a: Two nights and three days is the practical minimum; three nights gives a better chance of sightings.
Yes. A Forest Department permit is required and is usually arranged by your tour operator.
